terms.comment: Also singular, intestīnum, a gut. Ex intestīnīs labōrāre is to have trouble with one’s bowels (see bowels).
All the inner organs, heart, lungs and liver as well as the guts; in classical prose only plural (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: the nobler inner organs, heart, lungs and liver, above all those of a victim, from which the soothsayers foretold
evidence: Cic. Div. 2.28: aliōs enim aliō mōre vidēmus exta interpretārī (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Cum decimum jam diem graviter ex intestīnīs labōrārem…
phrases.english: When I had already been suffering badly with my guts for ten days…

phrases.latin: aliōs enim aliō mōre vidēmus exta interpretārī
phrases.english: for we see different people reading the entrails in different ways

viscus.html: De Vaan 683 heads the entry vīscus, -eris and prints vīscerātim and ēvīscerāre. Viscum, mistletoe and birdlime, is another word, with a short i.

sources: Lewis & Short: intestinus · Lewis & Short: viscus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 58, 334.
Lewis & Short: exta
